header.competitor: Fiserv, through the customer's bank (incumbent, which responded with a sharper rate)
header.tag_why: The rep calls this a price loss, but the evidence points to value proof. The CFO decided from a controller's one-pager that compared only rate lines, with our quote as the sole input from us. Nothing on the page put a dollar figure on the one-in-twelve failed orders. We passed up the chance to build one: Farah offered to run their declines from a three-month export, and the rep skipped it to save time. Lucy also asked for a one-page business case and got the deck and pricing proposal instead. The runner-up is Champion or access. We never met Martin; Lucy carried the deal into a room the rep wasn't in.

messaging_changes.current_line: Proven ROI, backed by an independent economic impact study.
messaging_changes.change: Replace the generic third-party ROI claim with a customer-specific offer, for example: 'Send us three months of declines and we'll show you, in dollars, what your failed checkouts cost.' Package the output as a one-page business case the champion can hand to finance.
messaging_changes.why: The decider only ever saw rate versus rate. Our ROI claim is an average from someone else's study, and it never reached the CFO as a Fernbrook number. The champion explicitly asked for something to hand him.
evidence_excerpts: She wanted a three-month export so she could show what the failed orders were worth.
Lucy asked once if we had something she could hand Martin.

messaging_changes.current_line: Customers see an average uplift in authorization rates with Authorization Boost and Adaptive Acceptance.
messaging_changes.change: Lead with the customer's problem instead of an average uplift statistic, for example: 'Stop losing your biggest orders at the last step.' Explain why high-value baskets get declined, then tie the fix to the customer's own decline data.
messaging_changes.why: What landed was Farah's specific explanation of why big-ticket orders get knocked back, not the average uplift slide. Lucy's own framing is about losing the largest orders at the final step. 'Average' invites a 'same thing' comparison.

messaging_changes.change: Add a line that moves finance from rate comparison to total cost, for example: 'The rate line isn't the cost. Compare what you lose to failed payments and what you pay to handle them.' Pair it with a CFO-facing comparison template that includes lost orders and the costs that never appear on the statement line.
messaging_changes.why: The incumbent's only move was a better rate, and the CFO framed us as 'the same thing.' Our messaging gives finance no counter to a like-for-like rate sheet. The gateway fee and chargeback headcount are the rep's claims and unverified, so the angle needs testing.

trigger.insight: This was a revenue-loss problem on high-value orders, measured by the customer, combined with frustration at an incumbent who couldn't explain it. We had the customer's own failure rate from day one and never converted it into a dollar figure. That is the gap that later decided the deal.
trigger.messaging: Open on lost revenue from failed checkouts, especially big baskets, and on getting a straight answer about why. Avoid generic global or currency positioning (M1), which didn't figure in this deal.

decider.insight: The ecommerce champion and IT were on board. The CFO decided alone, and everything we know about him came through Lucy. We accepted 'she'd carry it' but never gave her anything to carry beyond a deck and a price.
decider.messaging: When the decider is finance and won't meet vendors, our messaging has to travel without us. That means a one-page, finance-language business case the champion can present.

competitor.insight: The incumbent bank didn't compete on the problem; it only cut the rate. That one move changed the evaluation from 'why do big orders fail' to 'can you beat the rate.' We followed them onto price instead of pulling the conversation back to the failed orders.
competitor.messaging: Prepare a response to an incumbent rate cut that brings the conversation back to cost: 'a lower rate doesn't fix the one in twelve orders you're losing.'

message.insight: The decline explanation landed strongly with the champion. The silence question was deflected. The real silence was the CFO: our average uplift slide and customer stories never registered with him as anything different, so he called it 'the same thing.'
message.messaging: Keep the specific decline story, which worked. Stop relying on average-uplift and customer-story proof (M4, M8) as the business case for finance.

decided.insight: The deal was lost in a meeting we weren't in, on a page we didn't write, where our quote was the only thing from us. The rep blames the rate. Under questioning, though, he conceded that a matched rate would still leave 'same rate, so why move,' and that IT was nervous about moving before spring. Price was the visible symptom; the missing value case was the cause.
decided.messaging: Make sure our value shows up on the finance comparison page itself: the customer's lost-order cost next to the rate.

gaps.insight: The main gap was proof, not product. A customer-specific business case was requested and was within reach through Farah's analysis, but it was skipped for speed at quarter-end. The total-cost argument (gateway fee, chargeback headcount) existed only in the rep's head.
gaps.messaging: Make the 'we'll value your declines' analysis a standard offer, and build a finance-ready one-pager template.

language.insight: The champion speaks about lost sales on the biggest orders. The CFO, secondhand, speaks about undifferentiated sameness. Our words ('authorization rates', 'uplift', 'acceptance') match neither.
language.messaging: Use 'orders dying at the last step' and 'big baskets' framing in place of authorization-rate jargon. Directly counter 'the same thing' with customer-specific differences.

gaps.question: Which part of our pitch got silence?
gaps.follow_up: Ask the rep which slides or claims Lucy didn't react to or ask about, especially the average uplift slide and customer stories.

gaps.question: Did Martin ever see what the failed orders were costing?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Lucy, if possible, what she told Martin about the one-in-twelve failure rate and whether any cost figure was discussed.

gaps.question: How far apart were our rate and the bank's sharpened rate?
gaps.follow_up: Get the actual quote and the bank rate from the controller's comparison to size the price gap honestly.

gaps.question: How much did IT's concern about moving before spring weigh on the decision?
gaps.follow_up: Ask the rep or Lucy whether migration timing came up in the CFO meeting and whether a post-spring start was ever offered.

gaps.question: Are the gateway fee and dedicated chargeback headcount verified customer costs?
gaps.follow_up: Ask the rep where these came from (customer statement, Lucy, or assumption) and whether they could be quantified.

close.rep_takeaway: You had the customer's own failure rate and an SE ready to turn it into dollars, and you traded that for speed. When the decider is a CFO you can't meet, the champion needs a Fernbrook-specific business case before the rate comparison happens. More room on the rate wouldn't have changed the 'same thing' verdict.
